**TOP LINE**
H.R. 6500, the FY2027 continuing resolution, passed the Senate and returns to the House. Treasury's Fiscal Service and debt issuance operations remain exposed until enactment. H.R. 8595 and H.R. 9770, both received in the Senate, carry appropriations for TFI/OFAC and core departmental offices including IRS and FinCEN. Funding gaps across any of these vehicles would impair sanctions enforcement, tax administration, and cash management functions.

**NOMINATIONS**
Gadwood (IRS Chief Counsel) was referred to the full Senate at day 52. Four nominations remain stalled or cleared: Kothari returned at day 223; Korb and Trennert withdrawn at days 269 and 380 respectively; Petit withdrawn at day 549. IRS Chief Counsel and two Assistant Secretary slots remain unfilled.

**LEGISLATION & RULES**
Senate Finance received S. 5227 (First-Time Homebuyer) and S. 5216 (Senior Accessible Housing Tax Credit); House companions H.R. 7468 and H.R. 9554 also active. S. 3333 (Emergency Savings Enhancement) calendared in the Senate. All engage IRS administration and OTP scoring. FinCEN published a Geographic Targeting Order for Minnesota (Aug. 11). Backup withholding rules on third-party network transactions published Aug. 10.

**HEARINGS**
House Financial Services Subcommittee: FinCEN oversight hearing, witness Director Andrea Gacki.

# House Financial Services Committee – Democratic Member Prep Sheet
**Witness Topic:** Corporate Transparency Act / BOI, AML Modernization, Crypto Illicit Finance
**Note:** Public-source preparation aid only. Not official Treasury guidance.

---

## Maxine Waters (D-CA) – Ranking Member

**Line 1:** Waters will likely challenge Treasury on the current pause or litigation-related delays in BOI enforcement, framing non-enforcement as a gift to money launderers and shell company abusers. She may cite specific FinCEN enforcement gaps or reference the FATF mutual evaluation findings on U.S. beneficial ownership weaknesses.

**Line 2:** She will likely press on whether the Administration is adequately resourcing FinCEN to implement AML modernization under the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020, including whether the national AML/CFT priorities are being operationalized by financial institutions or remain aspirational.

**Suggested Posture:** Affirm Treasury's commitment to the statutory framework Congress enacted, cite specific AMLA implementation milestones achieved, and acknowledge enforcement challenges directly rather than deflecting. Waters rewards directness and reacts poorly to evasion. Offer concrete metrics where possible.

---

## Nydia M. Velázquez (D-NY)

**Line 1:** Velázquez is likely to focus on the impact of BOI reporting requirements on small businesses and minority-owned enterprises, particularly whether FinCEN outreach has reached non-English-speaking business communities and small LLCs in underserved urban markets.

**Line 2:** She will likely raise concerns about predatory shell companies and money laundering in New York real estate, including whether the Geographic Targeting Orders program is being expanded and whether BOI data will be usable by regulators to disrupt real estate-linked illicit finance.

**Suggested Posture:** Acknowledge the small business compliance burden explicitly and describe specific FinCEN outreach and education efforts, including multilingual resources. On real estate, reference GTO data and any interagency coordination with HUD or DOJ. Avoid overpromising enforcement timelines.

---

## Brad Sherman (D-CA)

**Line 1:** Sherman will almost certainly press hard on cryptocurrency and illicit finance, potentially citing specific cases involving North Korean hackers (Lazarus Group), ransomware payments, or Hamas/Iran sanctions evasion. He may challenge whether Treasury believes existing AML rules adequately cover DeFi and unhosted wallets.

**Line 2:** He is likely to question whether the crypto industry is receiving preferential regulatory treatment compared to banks, specifically whether Treasury is applying Bank Secrecy Act obligations to crypto asset service providers with the same rigor it applies to traditional financial institutions.

**Suggested Posture:** Be factual and specific on enforcement actions taken (OFAC designations, FinCEN enforcement orders). Acknowledge the regulatory gap debate around DeFi without prejudging ongoing rulemaking. Sherman is well-briefed on technical detail and will probe vague answers. Avoid broad dismissals of crypto risk.

---

## Gregory W. Meeks (D-NY)

**Line 1:** Meeks, as former Foreign Affairs Committee chair, will likely examine the international dimensions of AML and BOI, including whether U.S. beneficial ownership standards align with FATF Recommendations 24 and 25, and whether trading partners and correspondent banking relationships are affected by U.S. enforcement gaps.

**Line 2:** He may raise concerns about the impact of de-risking by large U.S. banks on Caribbean and African correspondent banking relationships, asking whether AML compliance burdens are driving financial exclusion in developing economies and what Treasury is doing to address that dynamic.

**Suggested Posture:** Engage substantively on FATF alignment and cite the 2024 mutual evaluation cycle. On de-risking, acknowledge the documented harm to remittance corridors and reference Treasury's interagency work on the subject. Avoid appearing dismissive of the correspondent banking access issue.

---

## Stephen F. Lynch (D-MA)

**Line 1:** Lynch, who has a long record on financial system oversight and has shown interest in both crypto and AML, will likely press on whether SAR (Suspicious Activity Report) data from crypto exchanges is being effectively used by law enforcement, and whether FinCEN's analytical capacity is keeping pace with transaction volume.

**Line 2:** He may question Treasury on the FinCEN Files-type concerns, specifically whether large financial institutions filing SARs are doing so as a genuine compliance function or as a legal shield, and whether Treasury has taken steps to improve SAR quality and utility.

**Suggested Posture:** Cite specific improvements to FinCEN's analytical infrastructure and any FinCEN Exchange public-private partnership outcomes. On SAR quality, acknowledge the problem honestly. Lynch appreciates oversight rigor and will follow up on non-answers. Do not suggest the SAR system is functioning optimally if the data does not support that claim.

---

## Al Green (D-TX)

**Line 1:** Green will likely connect the CTA and AML framework to fair lending and racial equity concerns, asking whether illicit finance enforcement disproportionately scrutinizes minority-owned businesses or minority communities while large financial institutions face limited accountability.

**Line 2:** He may press on whether the beneficial ownership database will be accessible to community banks, credit unions, and smaller financial institutions that serve underbanked communities, and whether there is a two-tier enforcement system favoring large institutions.

**Suggested Posture:** Acknowledge the civil rights dimension of financial regulation directly. Describe FinCEN access tiers for the BOI database and note that authorized financial institution access is part of the statutory framework. Commit to equitable enforcement. Green responds well to direct engagement on equity concerns and poorly to bureaucratic deflection.

---

## Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO)

**Line 1:** Cleaver, who has focused on predatory financial practices and community economic development, will likely ask how the CTA protects small community-based businesses from being exploited by larger shell company structures, and whether enforcement will prioritize bad actors over burdening legitimate small enterprises.

**Line 2:** He may raise concerns about the faith community and nonprofit sector, including whether religious organizations, community development organizations, or charities are being caught in AML compliance requirements in ways that impede legitimate charitable work.

**Suggested Posture:** Emphasize the exemptions built into the CTA for nonprofits and certain regulated entities. On small business burden, reference the 23 statutory exemptions and FinCEN's tiered approach. Cleaver is pastoral in tone and responds well to witness humility and acknowledgment of real-world compliance

bills.title: Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027
bills.status: Message on Senate action sent to the House.

The implementation risk centers on Treasury's ability to execute borrowing operations and agency payment processing without a lapse that could trigger cash flow constraints or disrupt Fiscal Service systems supporting government-wide appropriations accounting.

bills.status: Referred to the Committee on Appropriations, and in addition to the Committee on Education and Workforce, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.
bills.nexus: Without a known nexus to Treasury authorities or offices, this bill appears to fall primarily within the jurisdiction of the Committees on Appropriations and Education and Workforce, touching national service programming and labor market policy rather than tax, finance, or financial regulation functions. Treasury Legislative Affairs should monitor for any tax credit, bond financing, or payroll-related provisions that could engage IRS, OTA, or Fiscal Service equities during markup.

bills.title: Emergency Savings Enhancement Act of 2025
bills.status: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 544.
bills.nexus: S. 3333 would likely amend the Internal Revenue Code to expand or create tax-advantaged emergency savings mechanisms, directly implicating IRS rulemaking authority under the Office of Tax Policy and the IRS. Treasury's implementation risk centers on designing qualifying account rules, employer plan integration guidance, and potential revenue cost estimates that must be scored before floor consideration.

bills.title: First-Time Home Buyer Empowerment Act
bills.status: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
bills.nexus: S. 5227 falls squarely within Treasury's purview because any new first-time homebuyer tax credit or savings incentive would be administered by IRS and would require Office of Tax Policy to draft guidance and revenue estimates. The implementation risk centers on accurately scoring the cost of the credit, preventing improper claims at scale, and coordinating with HUD on eligibility definitions to avoid compliance gaps.

bills.title: Senior Accessible Housing Tax Credit Act of 2026
bills.status: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
bills.nexus: Treasury cares because S. 5216 would create a new tax credit administered through the Internal Revenue Code, directly implicating IRS's authority to design guidance, eligibility rules, and compliance mechanisms. The implementation risk centers on IRS and the Office of Tax Policy needing to define "accessible housing" standards, coordinate with HUD on qualifying criteria, and manage potential interactions with existing Low-Income Housing Tax Credit rules under Section 42.

bills.title: Making appropriations for national security, Department of State, and related programs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
bills.nexus: H.R. 8595 directly funds programs administered through Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence (TFI) and touches sanctions-related authorities under IEEPA and OFAC that depend on annual appropriations for staffing and operations. If the bill stalls or is amended in the Senate, Treasury faces the risk of a funding gap that could impair sanctions enforcement, financial intelligence activities, and interagency coordination on national security financial policy.

bills.title: Continuing Appropriations Act, 2027
bills.nexus: H.R. 9770 directly funds Treasury's annual operating appropriations, covering offices such as IRS, the Departmental Offices, and the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network through the continuing resolution period. Without enacted appropriations, Treasury faces operating constraints, potential lapses in tax administration and financial intelligence functions, and disruption to debt management operations under the authority of the Fiscal Assistant Secretary.

bills.title: Senior Accessible Housing Tax Credit Act of 2026
bills.status: Sponsor introductory remarks on measure. (CR H4413)
bills.nexus: H.R. 9554 proposes a new tax credit targeting senior housing construction and rehabilitation, directly engaging the Internal Revenue Service (under Treasury's supervision) and the Office of Tax Policy to design and administer eligibility rules, credit calculations, and compliance mechanisms. Treasury faces implementation risk in standing up a novel credit structure, including guidance issuance, potential interaction with existing Low-Income Housing Tax Credit provisions, and revenue cost estimation for scoring purposes.

bills.title: First-Time Home Buyer Empowerment Act
bills.status: Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
bills.nexus: H.R. 7468 falls under Treasury's purview because it would amend the Internal Revenue Code to create or expand a tax benefit for first-time homebuyers, directly engaging the IRS's administration of individual income tax provisions and the Office of Tax Policy's revenue-scoring responsibilities. The implementation risk centers on IRS's capacity to verify eligibility, design compliant forms and guidance, and absorb the revenue cost estimated by Joint Committee on Taxation.
